title: Optimizing costs and performance with Advanced Managed Scaling on Amazon EMR on EC2
key_points: EMR Advanced Scaling adds one dial on top of managed scaling: a utilisation-versus-performance index from conservative to aggressive.
Three runs of the same TPC-DS job show conservative settings avoid node churn for back-to-back jobs, while aggressive settings scale up fast for SLA-bound work.
Advice: start balanced, then tune while watching cost and runtime.
services: Amazon EMR
decision: Utilisation-optimised vs balanced vs performance-optimised scaling for EMR on EC2 clusters
authors: Amit Maindola, Bret Pontillo, Mukesh Punhani, Vishal Vyas

title: Lowering AWS KMS decrypt API costs in EMR Spark jobs
key_points: Every encrypted S3 object Spark reads costs a KMS decrypt call, so many small files quietly inflate the KMS bill, especially where Bucket Keys are ruled out for audit reasons.
Three levers: compact small files, use columnar compressed formats such as Iceberg/Parquet, and add Glue Data Catalog partition indexes so fewer objects are touched.
Each lever is checked by counting decrypt calls in CloudTrail before and after.
services: Amazon EMR, AWS KMS, Amazon S3, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Apache Iceberg
decision: S3 Bucket Keys vs file compaction vs partition indexes to cut KMS decrypt cost under audit constraints
authors: Navaneedha Krishnan Jagathesan

title: Deliver Apache Kafka data to streaming tables for Apache Iceberg with Amazon MSK Express brokers
key_points: MSK Express brokers can now continuously write a topic into a read-only Iceberg table on S3 Tables, with no connectors, Flink jobs or consumers to run.
Tables land in the Glue catalog, so Athena, Redshift and Spark can query them and stewards can add business context; raw delivery to ordinary S3 buckets is also offered.
AWS reports up to 60% lower cost than self-managed options and up to 30% lower downstream query cost from better file sizing.
services: Amazon MSK, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS Glue Data Catalog
decision: Broker-native delivery to streaming tables vs Kafka Connect Iceberg sink vs Flink for Kafka to Iceberg
authors: Shakhi Hali, Mazrim Mehrtens, Huyam Hasan

title: Accelerate Spark on EMR Serverless with larger workers and shuffle-optimized disks
key_points: EMR Serverless adds a larger worker (AWS reports 32 vCPU / 244 GB) that can attach large shuffle-optimised disks, aimed at shuffle-heavy and I/O-heavy Spark jobs.
AWS reports roughly 27-37% lower cost than small workers at the same total vCPUs on TPC-DS and TPC-H runs.
Argues disk should be sized for speed, not trimmed for cost, since slow shuffles are billed on the pricier vCPU and memory dimensions; lists when large workers do not help.
services: Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark
decision: Many small workers vs fewer large workers with shuffle-optimised disk for shuffle-heavy Spark
authors: Karthik Prabhakar, Arun Maniyan, Neil Mukerje

title: Build a contract compliance search system with Amazon OpenSearch
key_points: Builds contract search that finds clauses by meaning and then highlights the exact passages that answer the query, using semantic search plus a semantic highlighting model.
Deployed with two CloudFormation stacks and tested on synthetic contracts.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Lambda, Amazon S3
authors: Durga Prasad, Chanpreet Singh

title: Automate Spark Scala migration to 4.x with AWS Spark Upgrade Agent
key_points: Part 3 of the Spark Upgrade Agent series: an MCP-driven agent upgrades a Scala Spark 3.3 project to Spark 4.0 on EMR, updating build.sbt, Java version and deprecated APIs, then validates the job.
Scala-specific; the PySpark walkthrough is in Part 2.
services: Amazon EMR, AWS Spark Upgrade Agent, Apache Spark, Scala
authors: Bezuayehu Wate, Chuhan Liu, Keerthi Chadalavada, Prasad Nadig, Shubham Mehta, Karthik Prabhakar

title: Building a scalable personalized recommendation system on AWS: From batch to real-time
key_points: An Amazon.com team shares how its recommendation system started batch-first: shared golden datasets in a Lake Formation data lake, Airflow DAGs on MWAA chaining Athena, Glue and SageMaker steps, results served from DynamoDB.
Real-time signals were added later with vector search in MemoryDB rather than rebuilding the batch core.
Lessons on reliability, failure handling and keeping experiments cheap.
services: Amazon MWAA, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon Athena, AWS Glue, Amazon SageMaker, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon MemoryDB
decision: Batch-first precomputed serving vs real-time inference, and when to add the real-time path
authors: Amazon — Shraddha Anil Naik, Sergii Oborskyi, Walter Wong, Shawn Liu

title: Automate creating AWS Glue Data Catalog views with AWS SDK for data mesh use case
key_points: Glue Data Catalog views can now get their Athena dialect through the SDK, so one CreateTable call can create Athena and Spark versions of a view together.
A cross-account definer role holds the base-table access; consumers only see the view, shared through Lake Formation, which lets producers manage views from CI/CD.
Also shows adding the Athena dialect to older Spark-only views.
services: AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon Athena, AWS Glue, Amazon EMR
decision: Share base tables vs share multi-dialect catalog views with a definer role for cross-account data products
authors: Aarthi Srinivasan

title: Efficient log management with Amazon OpenSearch Service data streams
key_points: Data streams spread time-series writes over rolling backing indices, and ISM policies handle rollover, retention and moving older data to UltraWarm.
Basic setup steps for templates, the stream and ingestion.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Praveen Krishnamoorthy Ravikumar, JP Boreddy, Kevin Fallis, Aswin Vasudevan

title: How Alight Solutions achieved 55% cost savings with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Alight moved its logging platform from self-managed Elasticsearch to OpenSearch Service as its Elasticsearch version neared end of support.
Covers ingestion paths, buffering, security, the cut-over plan and lessons learned.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon OpenSearch Ingestion, Amazon ECS
authors: Alight Solutions — Mark Larson, Andrew Kummerow, Puneeth Komaragiri, Jagadish Kumar, Praful Kava, Tim Razik

title: Govern Amazon Redshift Data Warehouses Data Across Accounts using Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: Uses SageMaker Unified Studio as a data mesh layer over Redshift: producer accounts publish Redshift tables as catalog assets, consumer clusters subscribe, and access is granted through the studio instead of hand-made sharing.
Long console walkthrough: account association, Redshift connections and data sources, subscription targets, and checking the audit trail.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon Redshift, Redshift data sharing
decision: Manual cross-account Redshift datashares vs catalog-driven publish/subscribe in SageMaker Unified Studio
authors: Bandana Das, Anirban Saha, Sindi Cali, Stoyan Stoyanov, Viral Thakkar

title: Migrate from Apache Solr to Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
key_points: Short case for moving ageing Solr deployments to OpenSearch Serverless, now that Migration Assistant supports Solr 6 to 9 sources.
An AI assistant in the tool produces the migration plan, blockers and schema/query translation.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Migration Assistant for Amazon OpenSearch Service
authors: Jon Handler

title: Zero Copy access to Apache Iceberg tables in Amazon S3 from Salesforce Data 360 using the Iceberg REST endpoint from AWS Glue Data Catalog
key_points: Salesforce Data 360 can read Iceberg tables in S3 in place through the Glue Data Catalog Iceberg REST endpoint, with Lake Formation controlling access.
Mostly a partner setup walkthrough (IAM roles, Lake Formation grants, Data 360 federation config) rather than a design discussion.
services: AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Lake Formation, Apache Iceberg, Amazon S3, Amazon Athena, Salesforce Data 360
authors: Salesforce — Avijit Goswami, Bill Tarr, Pratik Das, Srividya Parthasarathy

title: High-performance Remote Shuffle Service on Amazon EMR with Apache Celeborn
key_points: Running Apache Celeborn as a remote shuffle service moves Spark shuffle data off executors, so Spot interruptions and scale-down no longer force upstream recomputation.
Decoupling shuffle storage lets compute be sized for the work instead of the shuffle, and helps with skewed jobs.
Deployable on EMR on EKS or EC2 with Grafana metrics; covers key client/server settings and production concerns.
services: Amazon EMR on EKS, Apache Celeborn, Apache Spark, Amazon EKS
decision: Local external shuffle vs remote shuffle service for Spot-heavy, shuffle-heavy Spark
authors: Suvojit Dasgupta, Avinash Desireddy, Melody Yang, Vishal Vyas

title: Patch perfect: Automating Amazon Redshift patch testing
key_points: A cluster patch, reboot or modification event triggers a Fargate test runner that checks JDBC/ODBC drivers, the catalog queries common SQL clients send, and your own critical queries.
First run stores baseline timings; later runs flag queries that got slower, with results kept in S3 and a pass/fail email.
Supports the practice of Dev/QA on the current patch track and production on trailing, giving evidence to request a rollback.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon EventBridge, AWS Lambda, AWS Fargate, Amazon SNS, Amazon S3
decision: Trust maintenance patches vs automated post-patch regression tests on a current-track Dev/QA cluster
authors: Eva Donaldson

title: Multi-cloud lakehouse architecture on AWS for Agentic AI, Part 1: Architecture and best practices
key_points: Reference design for letting AI agents query data spread across clouds, warehouses and SaaS: unify metadata in the Glue catalog, add a context layer and MCP servers, run agents on AgentCore.
Clear rules for when to use Iceberg REST catalog federation, query federation, or ingestion into AWS, with a trade-off table on freshness, cost, governance and operations.
Production pitfalls: federated metadata drift, unpredictable federated query latency, Gateway timeouts versus Runtime, unbounded agent memory.
services: AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Athena, AWS Lake Formation, Apache Iceberg, Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse
decision: Catalog federation vs query federation vs ingestion for giving AI agents access to multi-cloud data
authors: Sakti Mishra

title: How Razorpay Built Real-Time Anomaly Detection with Amazon MSK
key_points: Razorpay moved from static monitoring thresholds to a streaming anomaly platform: events on MSK, detection in Flink, historical baselines in ClickHouse.
A declarative rule language separates what to detect from how it runs, so teams add merchant-level alerts without new infrastructure.
Lessons cover multi-tenancy from day one and using one Kafka backbone for many consumers.
services: Amazon MSK, Apache Flink, ClickHouse
decision: Static thresholds vs streaming detection with learned baselines for high-cardinality alerting
authors: Razorpay — Narendra Kumar, Masudur Rahaman Sayem, Sundar Sankaranarayanan

title: Cut costs and simplify operations with writable warm storage in Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: A writable warm tier lets OpenSearch update historical indices in place instead of moving them back to hot and out again as UltraWarm requires.
Includes a cost comparison and guidance on writable warm versus UltraWarm; needs OpenSearch 3.3.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon S3
authors: Bharav Patel

title: Introducing Apache Spark Connect support in AWS Glue interactive sessions
key_points: Glue interactive sessions can now be Spark Connect sessions: write and debug PySpark in VS Code, PyCharm or a plain script, while execution happens on Glue against the real data.
Replaces the older Livy/REST kernel approach, so IDE debugging and linting work without local Spark or special kernels.
Practical notes: a new session type, a separate VPC endpoint for Spark Connect traffic, token refresh and the live Spark UI.
services: AWS Glue, Spark Connect, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
decision: Local Spark/Docker vs Livy interactive sessions vs Spark Connect to Glue for PySpark development
attaches_to: aws-bytes: File Layout Optimization (active, Glue PySpark dev loop)
authors: Zach Mitchell, Gaurav Krishnan, Vaibhav Naik, Shrey Malpani, Tom Olson

title: How BigBasket uses the Iceberg based lakehouse architecture on AWS to power lightning-fast grocery delivery across India
key_points: BigBasket replaced day-old reporting with a medallion lakehouse: DMS change capture into S3, Spark on EMR deduplicating into Iceberg, dbt on Trino for models, and gold marts served from Redshift.
Hot data stays in Redshift while history is queried in place with Athena; Lake Formation and the Glue catalog govern both.
Clickstream runs on a split path: Kinesis to OpenSearch for seconds-level reaction, a batch path through EMR into Redshift for complete history.
services: AWS DMS, Amazon EMR, Apache Iceberg, Amazon Redshift, Amazon Athena, dbt, Trino, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
decision: Redshift for hot gold data vs Athena/Trino over Iceberg for history in a hybrid lakehouse
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (medallion layers); aws-bytes: change data capture / lakehouse (later)
authors: BigBasket — Annie Mattoo, Anirudh Chawla, Naga Sandeep Grandhi, Vikram Kumar, Vineet Thapliyal

title: Serverless analytics pipelines using the Apache Spark engine in Amazon Athena
key_points: Athena's Spark engine now exposes an authenticated Spark Connect endpoint, so notebooks, VS Code or dbt can run Spark serverlessly without a cluster.
Three patterns: Jupyter exploration, local IDE development, and a scheduled dbt-spark job writing Iceberg tables with an Airflow DAG that starts and always terminates the session.
Adds per-session cost attribution, live Spark UI and Lake Formation-governed catalog access.
services: Amazon Athena, Apache Spark, Spark Connect, dbt, Apache Iceberg, Amazon MWAA
decision: dbt-athena (SQL) vs dbt-spark on Athena Spark vs Glue/EMR Serverless for Iceberg transformations
authors: Avichay Marciano, Vincent Gromakowski, Vova Nevski

title: Deploy modern data platforms in minutes with MDAA
key_points: MDAA is an open-source AWS framework where a governed data platform (lake, catalog, Lake Formation, Glue data quality, encryption, audit, data mesh) is described in YAML and expanded into infrastructure.
Governance is built in from the first deployment instead of added later; shown with a university system across many campuses.
AWS reports one example shrinking about 1,800 lines of CloudFormation to 45 lines of YAML.
services: MDAA, AWS Lake Formation, AWS Glue, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon Redshift, AWS CDK
decision: Hand-written IaC vs configuration-driven accelerator (MDAA) for standing up a governed data platform
authors: Sudeshna Dash, John Reynolds

title: Amazon Redshift RG: Faster and lower cost, Graviton-powered
key_points: Explains why the Graviton-based RG nodes are faster: SIMD-tuned vectorised execution, Nitro SSD caching, and a built-in lake scan layer that replaces the separate Spectrum fleet.
JIT Analyze collects statistics from Iceberg/Parquet files as queries run, fixing poor join plans on lake tables.
AWS reports up to 2.2x faster warehouse queries, up to 2.4x faster Iceberg queries, 30% lower price per vCPU and no per-TB lake scan charge versus RA3; Southwest Airlines, tombola and Qoala quoted.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift RG instances, Apache Iceberg, AWS Graviton
decision: Stay on RA3 vs move to RG vs Redshift Serverless for warehouse plus lake workloads
authors: Stefan Gromoll, Ankit Sahu, Mohammed Alkateb, Yousuf Hussain, Nita Shah, Sanket Hase, Jingbo Zhang

title: Accelerating log analytics at scale with AWS Glue and Apache Iceberg materialized views
key_points: Application logs flow from CloudWatch Logs through a Lambda parser and Firehose into an Iceberg table, deployed with one CloudFormation stack.
A Glue materialized view in the Data Catalog holds the pre-aggregated results; a scheduled Glue job recomputes it fully, so Athena dashboards read a small table instead of raw logs.
Failed records go to S3 for replay; S3 Tables is named as the managed alternative with native materialized views.
services: AWS Glue, AWS Glue materialized views, Apache Iceberg, Amazon Data Firehose, AWS Lambda, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Athena, AWS CloudFormation
decision: Query raw Iceberg tables vs Glue materialized view (full refresh) vs S3 Tables materialized views for repeated log aggregations
authors: Shinu Tharol

title: Run log analytics for a fraction of the cost with the new engine for Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: OpenSearch gets a log-analytics engine mode that stores data as Parquet and routes each query to DataFusion for aggregations or Lucene for search, in the same domain.
AWS reports up to 4x better price-performance and up to 70% lower storage cost, with PPL and SQL support and no extra premium.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Apache Parquet, Apache DataFusion
authors: Jagadish Kumar, Rohin Bhargava, Michael Supangkat

title: AI-powered performance recommendations for Amazon Redshift
key_points: Two scheduled Lambdas run a daily review of a Redshift Serverless workgroup: one gathers system-view diagnostics and CloudWatch metrics, the other asks a Bedrock model for ranked fixes that are emailed out.

The trick is pre-computing threshold signals (small inserts, disk spill, stale stats, missing QMR rules) and pairing them with metrics, so the model cites real tables and query IDs instead of generic advice.
Every recommendation carries a category, the triggering signal and a concrete SQL or config action; VACUUM/ALTER suggestions still need human review.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Lambda, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS, Amazon S3
decision: Manual system-view tuning reviews vs Advisor alone vs signal-based LLM recommendations for Redshift performance
attaches_to: dbt-pipelines (Redshift Serverless workgroup); aws-bytes: Redshift ETL failure alert (planned)
authors: Steve Phillips, Richard Raseley
